articles.title: Devon school's strict rules led to boy's death - coroner
articles.summary: Taylor Lee, from Plymouth, Devon, took his own life after struggling with school.
articles.body:
A school's strict rules contributed to the suicide of a 15-year-old boy and there is a risk of future deaths, a coroner had concluded.

An inquest at Exeter Coroner's Court heard Taylor Lee, a pupil at Ivybridge Community College, Devon, part of Westcountry Schools Trust, took his own life in November 2023.

Area coroner Alison Longhorn ruled the cause of Lee's death was suicide, but also concluded he struggled with what he perceived as unfair school sanctions.

Longhorn is preparing a rare Prevention of Future Deaths report. These are made when a coroner identifies circumstances which create a risk of future deaths.

The report will require action to be taken to prevent harm.

Lee, from Plymouth, died weeks after he complained publicly about the school's introduction of stricter rules about being on time for lessons.

Ivybridge Community College uses a system of what it described as "reset" and "reflection" - by which pupils are separated from their classmates for part or the whole of the school day.

If pupils arrived after the "late bell", they face being put in internal exclusion, sometimes known as "isolation".

Warning: this story contains references to suicide and self-harm

Before his death, Lee posted on a Facebook page for parents his concerns about the behaviour policy at Ivybridge Community College.

He wrote: "I have very strong views on the school itself due to, not only the mental health issues it has caused me, but also the un-logical system it has in place.

"I'm a Year 11 and I've sat through from Year 7 and watched the school change dramatically, and I think this is the worst I've ever seen it.

"On the second day back after being sent to reflection for being 47 seconds late to tutor... What they are doing to us inhumane... I, as a student alone, am sick of waking up every day and dreading it."

Lee complained to principal Rachel Hutchinson about what he felt were the unfair rules and he was suspended.

The inquest heard from PC Tonice Edkins, a school liaison officer with Devon and Cornwall Police, who had been working with Lee.

She described him as having "fragile mental health" and said his "frustrations with school" and "managing the stricter rules" were the main causes of his stress and anxiety.

The inquest heard that, although Lee, who lived with his family in Plymouth, was on the Special Educational Needs (SEND) register, teachers were not usually given any discretion if he was late to lessons.

Edkins told the court Lee felt as he was being "set up to fail".

Longhorn asked Edkins if she had contacted the school over her concerns for Lee's mental health.

The officer said that, after a series of meetings with Lee, she emailed assistant principal Amy Pearce, warning the impact of the school's "punitive approach'' could negatively effect the vulnerable pupils she was helping.

She expressed her fear that "shaming" young people with multiple sanctions could exacerbate mental health struggles, leading to children feeling they were "not good enough" and "worth less than others".

The inquest heard Edkins did not receive a reply to her email.

She said, as far as she was aware, no arrangements were made to help Lee in the stricter school environment.

The coroner asked what kind of response Edkins hoped for from the school.

Edkins said: "I would have thought just being a bit more compassionate and understanding towards someone struggling with self-esteem - for Taylor to receive a bit more compassion and understanding around that time."

A lawyer for Lee's family asked principal Rachel Hutchinson if this was a missed opportunity to consider the impact of the new behaviour policy on students like him. Hutchinson agreed it was.

Hutchinson said she felt Lee's SEND needs were "competently met" by the school, adding Lee "struggled with the culture" the leadership was trying to create.

Lee's mother, Michelle Lee, raised her concerns on 6 November 2023 about the number of resets and reflections he was being given.

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line .

Richard Brooks, a youth worker who met Lee several times in the autumn term, told the inquest he seemed "unhappy" and "apprehensive".

He said Lee told him "every day [at school] was a battle and it's exhausting".

The inquest heard that, in the month before Lee died, he broke down in tears at school on 2 October and told a member of staff he had self-harmed and was thinking about suicide.

Asked by the coroner what action the school took after this disclosure, Hutchinson said they contacted his parents and "kept a closer eye on him".

But the coroner concluded there was no evidence Lee's teachers were informed he had self-harmed or was having suicidal thoughts.

The family's counsel said Lee was "highly intelligent" and a "talented musician" who enjoyed spending time with his friends and skateboarding.

The inquest heard his parents found him unconscious in his bedroom. He died on 18 November 2023.

Longhorn concluded that, while Lee had experienced mental health issues for some time, his treatment at school and what he saw as unfair school sanctions had the most significant impact on his mood.

Longhorn said there was overwhelming evidence he struggled with the change in the rules and his experience at school "more than minimally contributed to his mental deterioration".

She said she would be making a Prevention of Future Deaths report because Ivybridge Community College did not consider the impact of stricter rules on students like Lee, and had not changed its behaviour policy since his death.

She said, should the same situation arise, she was not confident the college would not handle it correctly.

Addressing Lee's family, Longhorn said: "I'm sorry for your loss.

"I can see how much he meant to you and how much you miss him."

A spokesperson for the Westcountry Schools Trust said it would be "closely studying" the coroner's report.

It described Taylor Lee's death as "tragic" and said his loss was felt across the school community.

It said: "Over the past three years, the school's approach to safeguarding and behaviour has been inspected both by Ofsted and the local authority and has been deemed to meet all the required standards.

"However, neither the school nor the trust are complacent on such issues and amendments will be kept under careful review as a result of the coroner's report.

"We will be closely studying the coroner's report into the tragic death of Taylor Lee, which is still felt across the school community three years on."

articles.title: Arrests made in Mohamed Al Fayed probe in France, police say
articles.summary: The Ritz hotel in Paris, which is still owned by the Al Fayed family, is one of the properties searched by police.
articles.body:
French police have made arrests after three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, were searched in relation to an investigation into Mohamed Al Fayed's abuse.

The Paris prosecutor's office told the BBC that several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released.

In a confidential letter sent to survivors, the Metropolitan Police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in what is understood to be a joint operation between British and French authorities.

It is the first time any arrests have been made in relation to alleged abuse and trafficking by the former Harrods and Ritz owner.

Mohamed Al Fayed accused of multiple rapes by staff

Several victims of Al Fayed were also interviewed by French investigators, the prosecutor's office said.

It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into "allegations of human trafficking committed by an organized group, aggravated pimping committed by an organized group, and rape".

The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed.

The late Egyptian billionaire bought the Ritz Paris hotel in 1979, and it is still owned by the Al Fayed family.

The Villa Windsor in western Paris, another property involved in the search, was a holiday home for the Al Fayed family. It was previously the home of King Edward VIII, following his abdication, and his wife Wallis Simpson.

The Met shared this statement from French authorities with victims:

"At this stage of the proceedings, several victims have been interviewed by French investigators, and the investigations are being conducted in liaison with the British authorities.

"In this context, searches and evidence-gathering operations were carried out in mid-October 2026, notably within the Hotel Ritz in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, as well as at the Villa Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez, a former property of Mohamed Al Fayed, and at the Villa Windsor in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, in the presence of British investigators.

"Several suspects were taken into police custody, measures which were lifted following their interviews, specifically for the purpose of analyzing digital material seized during the search operations.

"The investigations are continuing under the direction of the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office."

A Met Police spokesperson confirmed its officers travelled to France in October and were present during the operation.

Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC documentary and podcast in September 2024.

One of the women featured in the documentary said she was sexually assaulted by Al Fayed at the Ritz hotel in Paris, while another woman said she had been raped by him at the Villa Windsor residence.

Since those allegations, more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.

Both brothers died without facing legal charges in relation to these allegations.

Earlier this year, Police Scotland said it was carrying out further investigations into allegations connected to Balnagown Estate.

In a statement, a force spokesperson said: "Three people have been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims.

"Our inquiries are ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

The Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors group said it welcomed the "significant developments" and cooperation between the Met and French authorities.

"We believe that all properties owned by Fayed should be investigated with the same thoroughness as those already searched, wherever they are located, to ensure that no potentially relevant evidence is overlooked," the group said.

"We hope these developments represent meaningful progress towards identifying and holding to account all those who facilitated, concealed or assisted his offending, wherever they operated."

The survivor advocacy group No One Above said: "France is treating this as organised human trafficking, led by specialists, with properties searched and evidence seized. That is what a serious investigation into a network looks like.

"Two years on, survivors are still waiting for the same from the Met. It is time the National Crime Agency took this investigation over."

The management of the Ritz Paris told AFP news agency that it "does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour" and that it was ready "to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities".

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line .

articles.title: David Walliams unmasked as mystery British celebrity facing sexual misconduct allegations, who took media organizations to court to stop his identity from being revealed
articles.summary: British comedian and children's author David Walliams has been identified as the celebrity who fought a lengthy legal battle to prevent two major media
articles.body: British comedian and children's author David Walliams has been identified as the celebrity who fought a lengthy legal battle to prevent two major media organisations from publishing sexual misconduct allegations against him.Walliams, 55, was previously referred to only as “PPT” in court proceedings as he sought to stop ITN and The Guardian from revealing his identity and reporting allegations that he had used his fame and influence to pursue inappropriate and exploitative sexual relationships with girls and young women over several years.The identity of the former Little Britain star was revealed on Tuesday after he failed to secure an injunction preventing publication of the allegations.Walliams had argued that identifying him publicly could have potentially fatal consequences, with his lawyers telling the High Court that he had attempted suicide twice in recent months and required psychiatric hospitalisation.Judge Matthew Nicklin rejected his bid to prevent the reports from being published, ruling that the public interest in allowing the media organizations to report their findings outweighed the arguments for maintaining the injunction.What are the accusations against David Wailliams?A joint investigation by The Guardian and ITV News, based on accounts from around 30 sources and supporting records, reported allegations involving multiple women. Two women claimed they first met Walliams when they were 15 and alleged that they were groomed. Other allegations included unsolicited messages and inappropriate behaviour towards young women.Walliams has denied sexual misconduct, predatory behaviour, harassment and workplace wrongdoing. He has acknowledged that some women with whom he had casual relationships in the past may have felt hurt, but denied abusing his power or breaking the law.The controversy has also affected his professional career. HarperCollins ended its publishing relationship with the author in 2025 following an internal investigation into allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards young female employees.Walliams had sought to keep his identity secret, arguing that publication would seriously worsen his mental health and put his life at risk. His legal team maintained that the consequences of identifying him could be devastating.However, the judge concluded that preventing publication would amount to a serious interference with press freedom. The court's decision did not establish whether the allegations against Walliams were true.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Almost all of Iran's oil revenue will dry up': Rubio warns as US tightens sanctions
articles.summary: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has warned that Iran could lose almost all its oil revenue as US sanctions and efforts to block Iranian oil shipments
articles.body: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has warned that Iran could lose almost all its oil revenue as US sanctions and efforts to block Iranian oil shipments intensify, saying the economic pressure on Tehran would become “even worse”.According to news agency ANI, Rubio said Iran had only a handful of oil shipments left at sea that had escaped the US blockade during the brief ceasefire and the period covered by the memorandum of understanding (MoU). Once these shipments are exhausted, “almost all of their oil revenue will dry up”, he said.He added that the US treasury department, led by Scott Bessent, was working with intelligence agencies to shut down channels Iran was using to bypass sanctions, including alternative trading arrangements involving Asian markets.Rubio described the economic pressure on Iran as “extraordinary”, saying the impact of sanctions would continue to compound.He accused Tehran's leadership of bringing the crisis upon its own people, calling it a “radical regime of lunatics” and alleging that its policies were “destroying their own country”. According to ANI, he said Washington was determined to prevent Iran from finding alternative ways to generate revenue and evade sanctions.On the military front, Washington has indicated that it is not planning to resume large-scale strikes on Iran for now. Rubio said the US did not see an immediate need for major military operations, arguing that the economic pressure campaign and naval blockade were already inflicting significant damage on Tehran.However, the US has not ruled out further military action. American forces carried out limited strikes on Iranian air defence and radar installations on Qeshm Island in recent days, with Washington describing them as defensive operations.Meanwhile, diplomatic efforts to end the conflict remain deadlocked, with the US and Iran holding sharply different positions on the conditions for a peace agreement.According to Reuters, Iran has proposed resuming negotiations within two days but wants Washington to first lift its naval blockade, ease sanctions and agree to end hostilities across all fronts.Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended the proposal, calling it the most reasonable offer on the table. However, Rubio has dismissed Tehran's conditions as “outrageous and ridiculous”, saying Iran was not serious about reaching a deal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Who is David Walliams? His career and controversies including Little Britain and BGT
articles.summary: The entertainer shot to fame on Little Britain and also has best-selling series of children's books.
articles.body:
David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.

A three-year investigation by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women for sexual purposes.

He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.

Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain, his comedy sketch show with Matt Lucas broadcast on the BBC.

Walliams published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008, and his stories soon became best-sellers and led to comparisons with Roald Dahl.

His 23 children's books have sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, but he was dropped by publisher HarperCollins in 2025 after allegations of inappropriate behaviour, which he denied.

In 2012, Walliams became a judge on Britain's Got Talent, and was voted best TV judge at the National TV Awards (NTAs) four times. He was replaced as a judge in 2022.

Before entering showbusiness, Walliams was born David Williams but changed his surname's spelling to avoid having the same name as another member of entertainment union Equity.

He was married to Dutch model Lara Stone from 2010 to 2015 and they have a son.

That hasn't stopped speculation about Walliams' sexuality. He has described himself as "bi-curious" and called his 2012 autobiography Camp David – but said he isn't attracted to men in the way he is to women.

Walliams and Lucas won a string of awards for Little Britain including three Baftas and two International Emmys, and the programme was watched by 10 million people in the UK.

But in the two decades since it ended, views about the show and what is and is not acceptable to joke about have radically altered. The programme has been criticised for its use of blackface and for stereotyping and mocking characters from minority and marginalised groups.

In the wake of the Black Lives Matter movement in 2020, Little Britain was removed from streaming services including BBC iPlayer, Netflix and BritBox.

Another of the duo's shows, 2010 airport comedy Come Fly With Me, was also removed from BritBox a decade after its original broadcast, due to the show's use of racial stereotypes and using make-up to portray people from other ethnic groups.

Little Britain was restored to iPlayer in 2022 with several scenes cut out. Walliams and Lucas said they had re-edited the show to "better reflect the changes in the cultural landscape since the show was made".

Not all the criticisms of Walliams have involved new standards being applied to older work.

Walliams had to apologise after two charity performances, during which he yanked down not only the trousers but also the underwear of actor Jeremy Edwards and music producer Mark Ronson.

In 2020, he was booed while hosting the NTAs after making a joke about Caroline Flack being out of work, at a time when she had stepped down from hosting Love Island and was waiting to appear in court, having been charged for actual bodily harm following a row with her boyfriend.

Later in 2022, he was replaced as a judge on Britain's Got Talent after a Guardian story about a leaked recording of Walliams making insulting remarks about contestants during breaks from filming.

In the incident, which happened in 2020, he spoke about a pensioner to whom he had taken a strong dislike and a woman who he described as "the slightly boring girl you would meet in the pub" who "you would want to have sex with, but then decide not to". He used much stronger language when talking about both.

Walliams apologised, explaining: "These were private conversations and - like most conversations with friends - were never intended to be shared. Nevertheless, I am sorry."

He sued the show's producers Freemantle for misuse of his private information and breaching data protection laws. An "amicable resolution" was reached, with the production company apologising for the recording being made public.

Further controversy came in June 2025, when it emerged that Walliams had given two Nazi salutes during the recording of BBC One's Would I Lie to You? Christmas special.

Banijay UK, which owned the show's production company Zeppotron, apologised, adding: "It was immediately acknowledged during the recording that this segment would not be broadcast under any circumstances." Walliams has never commented on the incident.

Then in December 2025, HarperCollins, the publisher of his hugely successful children's books, announced that following a change of CEO, the company would no longer look after new releases by Walliams.

He was dropped over allegations he had harassed female members of staff, with HarperCollins explaining that the company took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns".

The Daily Telegraph reported that an internal investigation had been opened the previous year after a complaint was made by a junior member of staff about his behaviour. This reportedly found that staff had been told to only meet Walliams in pairs and advised against going to his house.

Walliams' spokesperson responded by saying he "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately" and that he had "never been informed of any allegations raised against him" by the publisher.

Then in September 2026, HarperCollins doubled down by announcing that they were cutting all ties with Walliams and would no longer represent his back catalogue, meaning that when his books sold out in shops, they would not be replaced.

articles.title: PASTOR COREY BROOKS: How the welfare state broke the Black family, and how to fix it
articles.summary: Recently, I examined how welfare state incentives broke the Black family, and now Project H.O.O.D. fights fatherlessness on Chicago's South Side.
articles.body: Recently, I got into a disagreement with a friend of mine who told me that it was slavery and segregation that broke the Black family. I brought up Thomas Sowell and Shelby Steele. Both men are at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, and both have made compelling cases that it was the welfare state that broke up the Black family. The evidence is there. Steele has argued that Black Americans were the first group in this nation to have a form of socialism practiced upon them by federal, state and city governments. That is quite a damning insight when you think about it. After the civil rights victories in the 1960s, we had the Great Society and its War on Poverty, and what we saw was the shift from the pursuit of equal opportunity under the law to remedies based on race instead of the needs of individuals. When you treat a race instead of individuals, you end up with a permanent system of dependency because a race cannot lift itself up. In Steele’s view, this form of racialized socialism was rooted in White guilt — the pursuit of racial innocence by Whites — instead of Black development. This resulted in Blacks being treated not as free citizens but as a special class whose problems required permanent management by the state. In 1960, according to U.S. Census Bureau data (Table CH-3), only 22% of Black children lived and grew up in single-parent homes. That means four out of five lived in homes with both parents. This statistic comes nearly 100 years after slavery. However, after 30 years of programs and policies of dependency, the welfare state had expanded enormously and become institutionalized. The same census data shows that the number of Black children living in single-parent homes had more than tripled. We can argue over how much of that original 22% can be traced to the legacy of slavery, but there is no argument that the astronomical increase that followed was due heavily to the welfare programs of the 1960s. ELI STEELE: THE TERROR OF BEING CALLED RACIST IS CRUSHING FREE SPEECH IN AMERICA What these programs and policies of dependency did was change the incentives around work, marriage and fatherhood. And no racial group, especially Blacks who held their families together for generations through racial oppression, could survive this onslaught on the basic values that any human needs to survive and thrive. I know this intimately. I work on the South Side of Chicago, where roughly 80% of households have only one parent in the home. I’ve never met stronger women than the single mothers I know. They often have no help, and they often fail to understand the role that their government has played in promoting this culture — one that makes it so hard financially to escape. The Black family survived slavery, Jim Crow and every other form of legal oppression. It did not survive the War on Poverty’s rules. The numbers prove it. Steele’s point about socialism practiced upon us is not abstract here. Neither is Sowell’s analysis of the incentives at play. Federal, state and city programs have for decades offered more support when a man is absent than when he is present. When you pay a woman more for having children without a husband in the home than for having one, you get more children raised without fathers. That is not a mystery. That is cause and effect. The Black family survived slavery, Jim Crow and every other form of legal oppression. It did not survive the War on Poverty’s rules. The numbers prove it. DADS AREN’T OPTIONAL — AND AMERICA’S KIDS ARE PAYING THE BRUTAL PRICE Fatherlessness is the root of so much of what we see on these streets. Young men without fathers grow up looking for identity, discipline and affirmation elsewhere. Gangs fill the vacuum the state helped create. Violence follows. Girls grow up without a model of what a responsible man looks like, and the cycle continues. This is the lived result of the incentives Sowell has documented for decades. And these incentives — socialist incentives — did not exist under slavery or segregation. There was no White guilt then. I have spent years trying to be a father figure to boys who have never had one, teaching them to look someone in the eye, shake a hand, show up on time and earn what they receive. articles.title: Board of Peace says Israel's aid response after Gaza floods 'insufficent'
articles.summary: The group, formed by Trump, issues rare criticism of Israel, while also blaming Hamas for the suffering of civilians in Gaza.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has called on Israel to immediately allow all necessary humanitarian supplies into Gaza after rain flooded tens of thousands of tents.

The US-backed body, established to oversee the implementation of Trump's Gaza peace plan, acknowledged the steps now being considered by Israel, but said "the response remains insufficient".

Israel's military agency in charge of co-ordinating aid into Gaza said it had allowed in tens of thousands of tents and trucks with winter supplies, but added reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".

On Sunday, three children and a woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in the central Strip.

Most people in Gaza have been displaced because of Israel's military actions. Around 65% of the population, about 1.4 million people, now live in tents or makeshift shelters, the UN says.

Standing soaked in Gaza City, Mohammed Jneid told the AFP news agency that heavy rains hit from one side and sewage overflowed on them from the other, with the ground and tents no longer able to hold.

"We have nothing left, no bedding, no food, nothing," he said.

Sitting inside her tent, Islam Al Mobayed told AFP there were seven children there, five of them young.

"This is not life," she said. "We are exhausted, we are tired of this entire life."

In rare criticism of Israel, the Board of Peace said it had been urging the Israeli government to authorise the entry of essential goods for temporary shelter and water and sanitation infrastructure.

The Board added that delays in approving the entry of supplies "exacerbated the consequences of a foreseeable humanitarian challenge" and delayed the start of decommissioning weapons and transferring Hamas authority to a transitional government.

It also said Hamas's failure to disarm and transfer power had compounded the difficulties facing Gaza's civilians.

The UN's humanitarian agency OCHA said more than 150,000 tents were outside Gaza ready to go in, but aid efforts were constrained "by Israeli restrictions on the entry of supplies and equipment and funding shortfalls".

UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov said on Monday that stocks of essential shelter and winter items inside Gaza had been exhausted.

"Israeli authorities must immediately lift all restrictions on entry of the supplies," he said, adding "we have run out of time".

Israel's foreign ministry spokeswoman Michal Maayan on Monday said Israel had in recent months put in place a winter plan in coordination with the Board of Peace and international charities.

That plan has brought in more than 91,000 tents and 8,200-plus trucks with tarpaulins, blankets, winter clothing, and other equipment, according to Cogat, the Israeli military body responsible for aid.

Cogat said it would not allow in equipment that could be used for military purposes.

Maayon accused Hamas of hoarding aid, saying: "Hamas is responsible for the delays in making more progress in the Strip, and winter-related hardships are a consequence of Hamas's action and policy."

In response to the Board of Peace, Hamas said in a statement published on Palestinian media that its comment "presents a distorted account of the causes of the disaster". The group denied it was responsible for ceasefire delays, pointing to a statement in August from Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators that accused Israel of violations.

Hamas said Israeli restrictions prevent the entry of materials necessary for shelter and recovery - and added the Board as the ceasefire implementor should look at its own "serious shortcoming".

Under the deal to end the two-year-long war in October 2025, Hamas agreed to give up governance and its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the 60% of Gaza it still occupied. Israel, however, has insisted Hamas must fully disarm before withdrawal.

The dispute has left the next stages of the peace plan stalled, with both sides blaming each other.

The war in Gaza began after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 when around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.

The Israeli military campaign in response has killed 74,645 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable. More than 1,600 people have been killed since the ceasefire in October last year.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza since then.

articles.body: David Walliams’ lavish London home has come into the spotlight after the four-bedroom townhouse was listed for sale at a staggering £10.5 million, amid a major controversy surrounding allegations of inappropriate sexual behaviour towards teenage fans. The 55-year-old comedian, children’s author and former Britain’s Got Talent judge was named on November 10 by The Guardian and ITN following a High Court battle over an attempt to prevent the publication of the allegations.According to the reports, Walliams was accused of targeting girls and women, some as young as 15, for sexual purposes. He has denied the allegations.Located in the sought-after Regent’s Park neighbourhood of London, the sprawling townhouse was purchased by Walliams for £8.45 million in 2013, according to HM Land Registry records. The property, situated on Prince Albert Road, is reportedly being marketed for £10.5 million.While it remains unclear exactly when the property was first listed, its asking price was reduced at the beginning of October, according to a Rightmove listing. Official documents identify the owner as David Edward Williams, the comedian's real name. He uses the professional name David Walliams to avoid a name clash.The property is also listed as the service address for Little Britain Limited, where Walliams is identified as a person with significant control, according to Companies House records.Inside the luxurious townhouse overlooking Regent’s ParkThe estate agent's description presents the property as an imposing white stucco-fronted residence in one of London's most prestigious neighbourhoods, overlooking Regent’s Park and London Zoo and located close to Primrose Hill.Spread across multiple levels, the house reportedly covers approximately 4,527 square feet (421 square metres). According to the listing, it has been completely refurbished and extended by its current owner over the past five years.The property features elegant fireplaces, decorative cornicing, tall sash windows and a combination of period architecture and contemporary interiors. The estate agent also highlights its modern technology and carefully designed living spaces.Photographs of the interiors reveal several trophies displayed around the house, including Walliams' Pride of Britain Award, which he won in 2006, and his BBC Sports Personality gong from the same year.The listing describes the residence as offering an opportunity to experience elegant park-side living, combining traditional architectural features with modern comforts.Why David Walliams was named after a High Court battleWalliams' property listing has attracted attention at a time when the comedian is facing serious allegations. On November 10, The Guardian and ITN identified him as the celebrity who had sought legal protection to prevent the publication of allegations concerning inappropriate sexual behaviour.The legal proceedings reportedly involved claims that the celebrity posed a serious risk of suicide if publicly identified. However, a High Court judge ruled that this was not sufficient grounds to prevent the media organisations from publishing their reports.Following the ruling, both The Guardian and ITN named Walliams and published their accounts of the allegations. Walliams denies the claims against him.From Little Britain fame to Britain’s Got Talent and children's booksWalliams first rose to prominence in the early 2000s through the popular comedy sketch show Little Britain, which he created and performed alongside Matt Lucas. The show became a major success and established him as one of Britain's recognisable television comedians.He subsequently expanded his career into television presenting, judging and writing. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister Pralhad Joshi on Tuesday stepped up his attack on Congress over ethanol blending in petrol row and accused it of misleading the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Pralhad Joshi on Tuesday stepped up his attack on Congress over ethanol blending in petrol row and accused it of misleading the public over the issue.Talking to reporters, Joshi took a jibe at Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi and said that Congress is trying to stir up "bogus movement led by a bogus leader."“One must understand that this is all part of an effort to appease—not just the minorities, but also Rahul Gandhi. They keep saying things in his favour. The public understands this,” he said.“At a time when crude oil is so expensive—with a base price of Rs 53 for petrol, while ethanol costs between Rs 57 and Rs 71 if derived from maize—there is simply no commercial logic to their claims. We took this initiative to support our farmers and to help the nation become self-reliant, rather than remaining dependent on imports,” he said.Joshi also said that Congress had attempted to launch a campaign against the government on several issues, including electronic voting machines, infiltrators and Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.“Yet, the Congress party tried to stir up a movement—a bogus movement led by a bogus leader, Rahul Gandhi. They've tried everything: questioning EVMs, advocating for infiltrators, and even attacking Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The public has rejected all of this; they simply did not accept it,” Joshi said.“Just as you need specialised, high-end equipment to test for blood sugar levels or detect cancer, similar equipment and recognised laboratories are required for testing petrol and diesel,” he added.“And who introduced this concept of using specific equipment and recognised labs? It was these very people—back in 2005, during the UPA's tenure—who issued an SOP and introduced the 'Petrol and Diesel Order',” he further said.This comes after Karnataka minister Rizwan Arshad said that the state government stands by its report that oil companies are blending more than 20 per cent ethanol in petrol, despite the companies' rejection of the claim/During a press conference, Arshad said the Karnataka government had last Friday released a report stating that petrol samples from seven districts were tested, and most showed an Ethanol blend above 20 per cent, going up to 31.2 per cent. articles.title: In 2023, Scarlett Johansson took legal action after an AI app used her Black Widow footage and an imitation of her voice in an unauthorised advert; months later, she accused OpenAI of copying her voice for ChatGPT
articles.summary: Scarlett Johansson’s legal action over artificial intelligence misuse of her likeness and voice spans two separate disputes within seven months, one over
articles.body: Scarlett Johansson’s legal action over artificial intelligence misuse of her likeness and voice spans two separate disputes within seven months, one over an advertisement and one over a chatbot voice. In October 2023, her representatives acted after an image-generating app used genuine footage of her, alongside an imitated voice, in a social media promotion she never approved. By May 2024, she was accusing OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, of copying her voice after she turned down an invitation to provide it, an allegation chief executive Sam Altman rejected. Both cases were handled through lawyers rather than a court ruling.Scarlett Johansson fake advertisement: Black Widow footage, an imitated voice and a disclaimerAccording to The Guardian, an app called Lisa AI: 90's Yearbook & Avatar posted the 22-second advertisement on X, the platform formerly known as Twitter. It opened with a behind-the-scenes clip of Johansson on the set of the Marvel film Black Widow, in which she appears to greet viewers by name and invite them along. The screen then switched to generated photos resembling her, while a voice imitating the actor told viewers the app could also create images from text and even videos.Small print beneath the video says the images were produced by the app and have nothing to do with the person shown. Johansson’s team spotted the advertisement on 28 October 2023 and confirmed that she is not a spokesperson for the company. Her lawyer, Kevin Yorn, told Variety that the team does not take such matters lightly and would pursue every legal remedy available. The advertisement was taken down, though when The Guardian reported on 1 November 2023, several apps by the same developer were still listed on the App Store and Google Play.Tom Hanks and authors have also objected to artificial intelligence use of their names and workJohansson was not the only public figure to react in 2023. In October of that year, Tom Hanks wrote on Instagram that a dental plan had used an artificially generated image of him in a promotional video, warning fans that he had nothing to do with it. Authors, including the comedian Sarah Silverman, have sued OpenAI and Meta, the parent company of Facebook, for copyright infringement, claiming the companies’ models were trained on their work without consent.Nor was it the first time Johansson’s image had been used without her consent. In 2018, she told The Washington Post about deepfakes that add women’s faces to pornographic videos. Nothing, she said, can stop someone from pasting her image onto another body and making it look realistic, and she described the internet as virtually lawless, apart from American policies that apply only within the country.What Scarlett Johansson says happened when Sam Altman twice asked her to voice ChatGPTJohansson said in a statement provided to The Washington Post on 20 May 2024 that Altman asked her in September 2023 to be the voice of OpenAI’s conversational system. In her statement to CNBC, she said Altman told her that her voice could help bridge the gap between technology companies and creatives and make consumers more comfortable with the shift towards artificial intelligence. She declined after much consideration, for personal reasons.Nine months later, she said, friends, family and the public all remarked on how much the newest system, named Sky, sounded like her. Johansson told CNBC she was shocked, angry and in disbelief that Altman would pursue a voice so close to hers that her closest friends and news outlets could not tell the difference. She also pointed to Altman’s post of a single word, “her”, on the day OpenAI announced ChatGPT-4o, which she took as a hint that the resemblance was intentional. The word refers to the film in which she voiced Samantha, an assistant who forms an intimate relationship with a man.Altman contacted her agent again two days before the 13 May 2024 announcement, asking her to reconsider, she said. The system was released before they could connect.OpenAI says Sky belongs to another actress, but paused the voice and apologised to JohanssonAltman rejected the allegation in a statement reported by CNBC, saying Sky’s voice was “never intended to resemble hers”. He said OpenAI cast the voice actor behind Sky before any approach to Johansson. OpenAI had also said in a blog post on Sunday 19 May 2024 that Sky belongs to a different professional actress using her own natural speaking voice, and that it would not share the names of its voice performers, to protect their privacy.Out of respect for Johansson, Altman said, OpenAI paused the use of Sky’s voice in its products, adding that the company was sorry it had not communicated better. Reports said that OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Johansson’s statement.Why Scarlett Johansson wants transparency and new legislation to protect individual rightsJohansson told CNBC that the episode forced her to hire legal counsel, who wrote two letters to Altman and OpenAI setting out what the company had done and asking it to detail exactly how the Sky voice was created. She said OpenAI reluctantly agreed to take the voice down, which differs from Altman’s account of pausing it out of respect. The Washington Post reported on 20 May 2024 that she was threatening legal action against the company.She framed the dispute as part of a wider struggle over deepfakes and the protection of a person’s likeness, work and identity, saying these questions deserve absolute clarity. Johansson said she hoped for a resolution through transparency and the passage of appropriate legislation to protect individual rights. She had taken on a large company before: in 2021, she and Walt Disney settled a breach of contract lawsuit she had brought against the studio. No court ruling or settlement has been publicly reported for either the advertisement or the OpenAI dispute. OpenAI’s own timeline says it paused the Sky voice on 19 May 2024, four days after talks with Johansson’s team began.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Anti-gay laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
articles.summary: The ruling brings to an end an 11-year legal battle by dual-citizen Jason Jones.
articles.body:
A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.

London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."

The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."

Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.

It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.

Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.

Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.

The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.

Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.

The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.

Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".

Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.

"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."

Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

articles.title: Emma Watson joins Prince William’s United for Wildlife campaign in London, urging businesses to improve transparency as major tech, finance and transport companies step up efforts against illegal wildlife trade
articles.summary: Emma Watson joined Prince William and Benedict Cumberbatch at a United for Wildlife business forum in London on June 22, 2026, where she called on
articles.body: Emma Watson joined Prince William and Benedict Cumberbatch at a United for Wildlife business forum in London on June 22, 2026, where she called on businesses and brands to improve transparency and take greater responsibility for protecting the natural world. Held during London Climate Action Week, the gathering brought together business leaders and organisations to discuss tackling illegal wildlife trade. Speaking at the event, the actress highlighted the importance of storytelling, corporate accountability and innovation in driving environmental action, particularly among younger generations. The forum also marked 10 years of the Buckingham Palace Declaration, with more than 300 corporate members and partners now part of the coalition.Why did Emma Watson join Prince William's wildlife campaign in LondonAccording to People, Watson attended the business forum alongside Prince William, the Prince of Wales, and Benedict Cumberbatch. The gathering was organised by The Royal Foundation’s United for Wildlife and brought together representatives from different sectors to discuss their shared responsibility towards protecting the natural world.In a LinkedIn post about the event, United for Wildlife described the discussion as a conversation about "the natural world and our shared responsibility to protect it". Watson also has a previous association with Prince William's environmental work. In 2021, she presented the 'Fix Our Climate' award at the inaugural Earthshot Prize ceremony in London. The initiative, launched by the Prince of Wales, recognises solutions aimed at addressing environmental challenges, with winners in five categories receiving $1.4 million to support their work.What message did Emma Watson have for businesses and brandsSpeaking at the United for Wildlife business forum, Watson spoke about the influence businesses and brands can have through the way they communicate their environmental commitments. She said: "Storytelling is really powerful, and the story that you tell as a brand, and the transparency you have and the way that you talk around these issues, it matters."The actress also emphasised that these conversations were particularly important for younger people. "It matters to young people," she added. Watson encouraged business leaders to bring their personal values into their professional responsibilities and highlighted the role of technology and innovation in environmental protection. She also drew attention to the people working on the front lines of conservation, saying that those risking their lives to protect nature were the reason others could come together to discuss these issues.What is Prince William's United for Wildlife initiative, and when was it launchedAccording to an official announcement from The Royal Foundation's United for Wildlife, the June 22 forum marked 10 years since the launch of the Buckingham Palace Declaration in 2016. The initiative began with commitments from more than 40 corporations and agencies and has since expanded to more than 300 corporate members and partners. Founded in 2013 by Prince William, United for Wildlife works with law enforcement organisations, governments, non-governmental organisations, communities and private-sector partners to disrupt wildlife trafficking networks.The latest forum also introduced new commitments from companies across the technology, finance and transport sectors. Major digital platforms, including Amazon, Alibaba, Google, Meta, TikTok, eBay, Etsy, Pinterest and Baidu, committed publicly to working towards ending illegal wildlife trade listings on their platforms. Their collaboration will explore AI-enabled detection and prevention methods. According to the announcement, the participating platforms represent approximately 33% of the global e-commerce market and reach more than 90% of the world's social media users.How will PayPal and Chainalysis help track financial activity linked to wildlife crimeThe financial sector also featured in the announcements, with cryptocurrency companies committing to disrupt the financial flows associated with illegal wildlife trade. Organisations including PayPal, TRM Labs, Chainalysis, Circle and Luno are joining efforts under the Mansion House Declaration. The initiative will establish a dedicated working group to identify suspicious financial activity, develop indicators of trafficker behaviour and coordinate investigations with law enforcement agencies.Transport and telecommunications companies also announced measures as part of the campaign. British Airways is launching a pilot public awareness campaign at Heathrow, with plans to expand it through in-flight entertainment and short episodes highlighting frontline environmental defenders. Vodafone, together with Vodacom and Safaricom, will use artificial intelligence and transaction-monitoring systems across M-Pesa to identify financial transactions linked to wildlife trafficking. The official announcement stated that the platform reaches 72 million customers in East Africa. These commitments form part of United for Wildlife's wider effort to strengthen cooperation between businesses and organisations working to prevent illegal wildlife trade.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Amazon villagers living along Brazil’s Lower Amazon say green anacondas are increasingly becoming a threat to their poultry, entering chicken coops and
articles.body: Amazon villagers living along Brazil’s Lower Amazon say green anacondas are increasingly becoming a threat to their poultry, entering chicken coops and swallowing birds. A study based on interviews with residents of five riverside communities in Pará has examined how these encounters shape people’s attitudes towards the giant snakes. Researchers found that the loss of domestic animals, rather than fear alone, was the leading reason residents gave for killing anacondas. The findings also document local knowledge of the reptiles’ behaviour, traditional beliefs surrounding a mythical Great Snake and practical suggestions for protecting poultry, including reinforcing coops with mesh.Why Amazon villagers are killing giant anacondas over stolen chickensThe research, titled The myth of the serpent: from the Great Snake to the henhouse, was published in Frontiers in Amphibian and Reptile Science on June 16, 2025. It was conducted in the Aritapera region of Santarém municipality in Brazil’s Pará state, focusing on five communities: Água Preta, Carapanatuba, Centro do Aritapera, Costa do Aritapera and Cabeça D’Onça.Researchers spent 64 days in the region in 2023, conducting interviews and recording conversations with residents. The study examined their experiences with anacondas, including encounters near homes, poultry losses, hunting practices and traditional beliefs.The findings showed that economic losses were the strongest reported motivation for killing the snakes. Protecting domestic animals, particularly chickens and chicks, accounted for 47.7% of the reported reasons. Personal safety accounted for 15.9%, the search for anaconda fat for 13.3%, fear for 6.8%, and the historical trade in snakeskin for another 15.9%.Residents described the frustration of spending time and money raising poultry only to lose birds to anacondas. One person interviewed by the researchers recalled finding a chicken inside a snake that had swallowed it moments earlier.How giant anacondas enter chicken coopsAccording to residents, anacondas can enter poultry enclosures through small openings and gaps. Their ability to squeeze through narrow spaces makes ordinary structures less reliable as protection.The researchers recorded accounts of snakes entering coops to prey on chickens and ducks. Residents also described how an anaconda could struggle to leave through the same opening after swallowing a bird because its body expands around the meal.The study noted that keeping poultry inside enclosures can make it harder for snakes to reach them, but existing coops do not always prevent attacks. In some cases, the structures may trap an anaconda inside after it has fed, creating another source of conflict with residents.The researchers found that encounters around homes and chicken coops generally involved smaller snakes than those reported in waterways. Residents described anacondas seen near houses as averaging around 2.3 metres in length. These measurements came from local accounts rather than direct measurements of a surveyed snake population.Researchers suggest simple chicken coop changes to prevent attacksThe study identifies stronger poultry enclosures as one of the most practical ways to reduce conflict between residents and anacondas. Rather than relying on killing the snakes, the researchers recommend modifying coop structures to prevent them from entering.Their analysis found that enclosures with closely spaced slats, covered with fine nylon mesh and an additional outer layer of plastic aviary grid, offered the best protection among the structures examined.The closely spaced slats help eliminate gaps through which snakes could pass. The nylon mesh acts as another barrier, while the outer grid protects the mesh from damage and helps block larger animals.The researchers said that because anacondas can squeeze through surprisingly small openings, the spacing between the structural elements is important. The proposed design aims to protect poultry while allowing the snakes to remain in their natural habitat.The researchers described improved henhouses as a promising first step towards reducing the number of anacondas killed in the region. Their findings also point to the need for conservation strategies developed in collaboration with local communities.The Great Snake legend still shapes local perceptionsThe research also explored the cultural relationship between residents and anacondas. In Amazonian folklore, the giant snake is associated with legends such as the Cobra Grande, or Great Snake, a mythical creature believed to inhabit the Amazon River.Some residents described the legendary creature as an enormous snake with eyes that appear to glow like fire in the darkness. The researchers recorded seven accounts from people who said they had seen, or knew someone who had seen, signs of the Great Snake.However, the study found that everyday encounters increasingly shape how residents view anacondas. Rather than seeing them primarily through the lens of folklore, many now regard them as a threat to their poultry and household income.Residents also demonstrated detailed knowledge of the reptiles’ behaviour, including their feeding habits, preferred habitats and seasonal appearances. They reported seeing anacondas more frequently during periods of flooding, when water levels rise across the surrounding floodplains.Amazon villagers believe anaconda numbers have declinedAnother finding concerned residents’ perceptions of the reptiles’ presence in the region. Across all five communities, many interviewees said they encountered fewer anacondas than in previous years.The proportion of accounts indicating a perceived decline ranged from 78.6% in Carapanatuba to 94.4% in Água Preta. These figures reflect residents’ observations and do not represent a scientific population survey.Interviewees suggested several possible explanations, including hunting, the loss of vegetation in wetland habitats, changes in flood levels, riverbank sedimentation and the expansion of settlements. Some also associated fewer sightings with changes in local poultry-keeping practices.The researchers noted that hunting for skins had historically been practised in the region, while killing anacondas to protect livestock remains a source of conflict. They also highlighted the role of habitat changes in shaping where the snakes are encountered.Conservation efforts need to address local livelihoodsThe study argues that protecting anacondas will require more than asking residents not to kill them. Since poultry losses are a major source of conflict, conservation efforts must also address the economic concerns of households that depend on raising domestic animals.The researchers suggest combining better-designed henhouses with community-led conservation measures and greater recognition of local knowledge. They also discuss the possibility of developing a management framework around the traditional use or trade of anaconda fat, an animal-derived remedy used by some residents.Their central finding is that reducing encounters around homes could help protect both poultry and anacondas. By making chicken coops more secure, communities may have fewer reasons to kill the snakes, shifting the relationship away from conflict and towards coexistence.You use AI every day. articles.title: Stevie Wonder tips Stalybridge cafe staff £1,000
articles.summary: Stevie Wonder went to Cafe Continental in Staley Bridge after his gig at the Co-op Live on Sunday.
articles.body:
Staff at a Greater Manchester cafe found themselves sharing a £1,000 tip after a late-night visit from a musical legend.

Cafe Continental in Stalybridge found itself feeding Stevie Wonder, his band and entourage after the singer's sold-out gig performing his classic album Songs In The Key Of Life at the Co-op Live in Manchester.

Owner Ryan Robinson said Wonder, 76, was "a really nice guy, happy to chat to everybody".

Among those dining was Wonder's daughter and backing singer Aisha, about whom he wrote Isn't She Lovely? for the album.

Robinson said he had been contacted about 18 months ago by members of the band, who called in while playing in soul singer Toni Braxton's backing band.

They stayed in touch, and then on Sunday, Robinson got a call to ask if they could come back after the show.

"The band turned up at 23:00 had some food and then at about 00:30, four blacked out mini buses turned up outside, and Stevie Wonder was in one of them," he said.

The cafe staff had been forewarned that they would need to work late and put on a different menu to the usual Sunday roast.

The singer had a seaside feast with grilled sea bream, bouillabaisse and octopus.

And the staff's efforts were rewarded with the generous tip from Wonder and his band.

"That was first for everyone," Robinson said, adding: "His family, his entourage and his crew are absolutely lovely.

"You wouldn't even think they were famous and they're really enthusiastic about the restaurant."

Robinson said he believed the band had found the cafe, which opened two years ago, on social media.

"If it wasn't for social media, they more than likely may have Googled something nearby and it might have led them to the city centre.

"But it's brought them out here into the suburbs and it's been really nice to see," he said.

"It's good for the area. For a small independent business like us to receive so much traction from this... getting such a major celebrity to this town itself, it does a lot."

articles.title: IBM ending visa sponsorship for most roles in IBM Consulting: What will happen to employees?
articles.summary: Tech giant IBM has announced that it is ending certain Green Card sponsorship and H-1B visa programs within its consulting business.
articles.body: Tech giant IBM has announced that it is ending certain Green Card sponsorship and H-1B visa programs within its consulting business. The company said that the decision has been prompted by skill availability in the US, meaning the company does not need to bring in foreign skilled workers. This does not apply to the entire company but only to IBM Consulting, which employs 150,000 people globally.IBM Consulting is the services and technology-advisory arm of IBM (International Business Machines). It helps other companies modernise their businesses, adopt new technologies and manage large-scale IT operations. It basically covers IT consulting, AI, cloud computing, cybersecurity, and business transformation etc. The workforce comprises software engineers and developers, IT consultants, data scientists and AI specialists, cloud architects, cybersecurity professionals, project managers and business analysts.'Funny how corporate calculus changes'Inspector General of the US Department of Labor, Anthony D'Esposito, reacted to the announcement and called it funny. He said the announcement was obviously a reaction to the Trump administration's crackdown on visa and Green Card abuse. "@IBMis pulling back on visa sponsorships. Funny how the corporate calculus changes when scrutiny shows up...If your business model depends on nobody checking, find a new business model," he said.What will happen to affected employees?Bloomberg reported that the affected employees will have the option to leave the US and continue working for IBM outside the US or leave the company at the end of the year.Will all H-1B visa holders of IBM be laid off?Many aspects of IBM's announcement remain unclear: like whether the announcement is for new sponsorships of Green Cards or whether those who are in the Green Card queue will be affected.1. Employees currently on H-1B visasIf they want to remain in the US, they will have to find a new employer as IBM is likely to stop their visa sponsorship.2. Employees whose Green Card applications are in progressThere are different stages in the employment-based Green Card process. If PERM is not filed, the employee may have to find another employer to start the process from scratch.If the PERM application is pending, a new employer generally has to begin its own PERM process.If PERM is approved but I-140 is not filed, then the employee will generally need a new employer to file a fresh Green Card petition.If the I-140 is pending, then the employee may also need a new employer to restart the process. There are limited protections if an associated I-485 has already been pending for 180 days.If the I-140 is approved, then the employee may retain the original priority date, even if IBM withdraws the petition, subject to USCIS rules.If the I-485 is pending for 180 days or more, the employee may qualify to transfer the Green Card application to another employer, provided the new job is in the same or a similar occupational classification.You use AI every day. articles.title: US Army soldier suspected of spying for Russia arrested in UK
articles.summary: The 41-year-old senior soldier is accused of national security offences and is being questioned in London.
articles.body:
A soldier in the US Army has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, British counter-terror police have said.

The 41-year-old senior serviceman was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday.

Counter Terrorism Policing London said the man had been arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023.

Section one of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while section three relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire.

The BBC understands the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC) , a strategic operational base for the alliance.

Counter Terrorism Policing said it was not linked to any other ongoing investigations.

FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement: "This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies."

He added: "While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, from Counter Terrorism Policing London, described the arrest as "significant".

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," she said.

The unnamed soldier is currently in custody at a London police station.

He has been detained under the National Security Act 2023, allowing police to hold him without charge for up to 14 days.

Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said: "The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.

"I encourage anyone who thinks they've witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office."

Additional reporting by Daniel Sandford, UK correspondent.

articles.title: A Circle K worker found a customer’s abandoned Arizona lottery ticket, clocked out and bought it himself; it turned out to be worth $12.8 million, and now a judge says the fight over who owns it can go ahead
articles.summary: A customer walked into a convenience store in Arizona to buy lottery tickets, ran short of cash and left some of them behind.
articles.body: A customer walked into a convenience store in Arizona to buy lottery tickets, ran short of cash and left some of them behind. By the next morning, one of those unpaid tickets had become a multimillion-dollar mystery. A store manager who discovered that it matched all six winning numbers decided to buy it himself after clocking out, removing his uniform and paying $10. The ticket was worth nearly $12.8 million. But instead of collecting a fortune, the employee found himself in a legal battle with his former employer, Circle K, over who actually owned the winning slip. Now, nearly a year after the drawing, a judge has allowed the dispute to move forward, according to a report by NBC Palm Springs, although the question of who gets the money remains unanswered.The case centres on Robert Gawlitza, a former manager at a Circle K convenience store near 56th Street and Bell Road in Scottsdale, Arizona. The winning ticket belonged to The Pick, an Arizona Lottery game in which players must match six numbers drawn to win the jackpot.According to court filings, the incident began on November 24, 2025, when a customer asked a store employee to print $85 worth of lottery tickets. She paid $60 but did not have enough money to cover the remaining $25 worth. The unpaid tickets were left at the store. That evening, the lottery announced its winning numbers, and one of the tickets left behind matched all six.Manager clocked out before buying the ticketWhen Gawlitza arrived for work the following morning, he learnt that a winning ticket had been printed at his store. He checked the remaining tickets and discovered that one was the jackpot winner. According to Circle K's lawsuit, he then clocked out, removed his uniform and asked another employee, Marline Ybarra, to ring up the purchase.Gawlitza paid $10 and received a receipt. He also signed the back of the winning ticket, with Ybarra reportedly signing it as well. The former manager later maintained that he had followed an established store practice requiring employees to purchase accidentally printed or unpaid lottery tickets.His lawyer, Josh Kolsrud, argued that the company had an unofficial policy under which workers were expected to buy tickets accidentally printed in excess of $20. The practice allegedly helped the retailer avoid losses from tickets that customers did not pay for. In July, Gawlitza's legal team submitted affidavits from six current and former employees who reportedly supported his account of the policy.Gawlitza said he had purchased the ticket legitimately and that the company challenged his ownership only after discovering its value. He and Ybarra had also agreed to split the winnings equally, according to their lawyer.Circle K is challenging the winCircle K, however, has a different interpretation of what happened. The company argues that the tickets were printed at its store but never validly sold to the customer or the manager. It has cited Arizona Lottery administrative rules that give retailers ownership of tickets that are overprinted or remain unsold. In February 2026, the convenience store chain filed a lawsuit in Maricopa County Superior Court, asking a judge to determine who legally owns the winning ticket and is entitled to the prize. The company has said the lawsuit is intended to clarify ownership rather than target a particular employee.There is another complication: the original customer, identified in court documents as Kim, has also emerged as a potential claimant. The central question is whether she abandoned the unpaid tickets or merely left them behind after being unable to pay for the full order. That distinction could prove important in determining whether she retained any claim to the winning ticket.The Arizona Lottery has been holding the prize while the legal dispute plays out. A judge previously extended the deadline for claiming the jackpot, which would otherwise have expired under the lottery's usual 180-day rule.Judge allows the ownership battle to continueThe latest development came on November 6, when Maricopa County Superior Court Judge Joseph Kreamer ruled that the legal case could proceed. However, he narrowed the immediate proceedings to the question of who owns the winning ticket. Most of the other claims, including those connected to the former manager's employment dispute, have been put on hold until the ownership issue is resolved.Gawlitza has also challenged the company's decision to fire him after the incident, arguing that he followed the store's established procedures. Circle K, meanwhile, maintains that the ticket was never validly transferred to him. The court will have to determine whether the $10 transaction constituted a legitimate purchase and whether the original customer or retailer retained ownership. For now, the nearly $12.8 million prize remains out of reach.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
