articles.title: A Florida wedding venue accused neighbours of disrupting ceremonies with gunfire, chainsaws and revving airboats, and won a court order to stop them; in October 2026, an appeals court overturned the temporary ban
articles.summary: A wedding ceremony is supposed to be a peaceful celebration, but a Florida wedding venue found itself dealing with a very different kind of disturbance.
articles.body: A wedding ceremony is supposed to be a peaceful celebration, but a Florida wedding venue found itself dealing with a very different kind of disturbance. Its owners accused their neighbours of repeatedly disrupting ceremonies with loud gunfire, revving chainsaw and airboat engines, loud music and roaming dogs. The alleged disturbances became the subject of a legal dispute after the venue claimed that the behaviour was interfering with its business and threatening its future.The Florida Sixth District Court of Appeal addressed the dispute in its October 30, 2026, decision in Brad Hatcher and Audrey Hatcher v. Restorical, LLC, doing business as Sydonie Mansion. The ruling, available on Justia, overturned a temporary injunction that had restricted the neighbours' conduct during weddings and other events. The appeals court found that although there was evidence supporting a harmful nuisance claim, the venue had not sufficiently demonstrated that it would suffer irreparable harm without the restrictions.Dispute over wedding ceremonies at historic Florida mansionThe case involved Sydonie Mansion, a historic property in Mount Dora, Florida, owned by Restorical LLC. The venue's owners, Clark and Amy Frogley, also lived at the mansion and had hosted weddings and other events there for approximately nine years. During its busy season, running from September through May, the business typically organised two to three weddings each week. However, Restorical claimed that activities on the neighbouring property, owned by Brad and Audrey Hatcher, increasingly interfered with these celebrations.According to the court's account, the alleged disturbances had occurred occasionally before 2025. These included playing loud music through speakers directed towards the mansion and allowing dogs to roam freely onto the venue's grounds. Restorical alleged that the situation became more serious in 2025, when the neighbours repeatedly engaged in noisy activities during scheduled weddings. These reportedly included rapid gunfire, revving chainsaw and airboat engines, operating chainsaws and releasing dogs.The company argued that the timing of these activities disrupted ceremonies and affected the atmosphere expected by couples and their guests. It subsequently filed a lawsuit against the Hatchers, including a private nuisance claim, and sought a temporary injunction to prevent further disturbances.Lower court granted temporary restrictionsFollowing an evidentiary hearing at which both sides presented testimony, the trial court granted Restorical's request for a temporary injunction. The lower court found that the neighbours' alleged conduct had caused continuing disruption to the wedding business and threatened the venue's goodwill and long-term viability. It also concluded that the resulting harm could not be adequately addressed through monetary damages.The injunction prohibited the Hatchers from disrupting the venue's scheduled events. It also required Restorical to provide them with written notice at least 24 hours before each event. The neighbours challenged the order before the Florida Sixth District Court of Appeal, arguing against the restrictions imposed on their property-related activities.Why the appeals court reversed the temporary banThe appeals court examined whether Restorical had satisfied the legal requirements for obtaining a temporary injunction. Under Florida law, a party seeking such relief must establish four elements: a substantial likelihood of success on the merits, the absence of an adequate remedy at law, a likelihood of irreparable harm without the injunction and consistency with the public interest.The court explained that failure to establish even one of these requirements is enough to deny temporary injunctive relief. In this case, the judges focused on irreparable harm and whether monetary compensation could provide an adequate remedy. They found that the evidence did not sufficiently establish that the alleged disruptions would cause losses that could not be calculated or compensated financially.Although Amy Frogley testified that she feared losing wedding bookings and potentially the historic mansion if the business could no longer generate enough revenue to maintain it, the court found that these concerns were not supported by sufficient evidence. There was no testimony or other evidence showing that weddings had been cancelled, bookings had been lost or substantial business losses were imminent. The court also noted that Restorical had operated the venue for nine years, giving it a business history from which potential financial losses could be assessed.At the time of the hearing, the venue was still accepting wedding bookings and was not informing prospective customers about the alleged disruptions. Although one incident had reportedly resulted in a partial refund of a wedding fee, there was no evidence that similar refunds would become frequent or create unquantifiable losses. The judges therefore concluded that the trial court's finding of irreparable harm was not supported by competent, substantial evidence.Nuisance claim remains openThe appeals court clarified that its decision did not establish that the neighbours' alleged behaviour was acceptable. It acknowledged that the evidence could support a finding that their conduct constituted a harmful nuisance. However, proving that behaviour amounts to a nuisance is different from satisfying the additional legal requirements for an immediate temporary injunction.The court reversed the injunction and remanded the case to the lower court for further proceedings. It also made clear that Restorical could still attempt to establish irreparable harm through sufficient evidence. The October 30 ruling did not finally resolve the underlying lawsuit or determine the parties' ultimate liability. Instead, it addressed whether the evidence justified imposing temporary restrictions while the legal dispute continued.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An Ohio woman withheld taxes from workers at her husband's electrical business but used company money on a Florida condo and vacations; after more than $494,000 went unpaid, she received an 18-month sentence
articles.summary: An Ohio woman who used hundreds of thousands of dollars in employee tax payments to fund a luxury lifestyle has been sentenced to 18 months in federal
articles.body: An Ohio woman who used hundreds of thousands of dollars in employee tax payments to fund a luxury lifestyle has been sentenced to 18 months in federal prison. Tammy Butdorf, 51, was sentenced in federal court in Akron after being found guilty of failing to pay employment taxes withheld from workers at her husband's electrical contracting business. This was confirmed in an official statement released by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Ohio. Butdorf worked as the accountant and office manager for the family business. Her duties included collecting federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare payments from employees' wages and sending the money to the government. However, an investigation by the Cleveland office of the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) found that she had been moving the money into private accounts over a period of six years. Between 2015 and 2021, Butdorf failed to send more than $494,000 (£380,000) in required quarterly employment taxes to the federal government.Misdirected funds spent on property and private clubsCourt records show that instead of sending the withheld payroll taxes to the Internal Revenue Service, Butdorf made payments directly to herself and her husband. Federal prosecutors said the money was used to pay for personal and family expenses. One of the purchases made with the unpaid tax money was a condominium in Florida. Investigators also found that the diverted payroll money was used to pay membership fees at a private camp, cover costs for a shooting club, and fund family holidays. Under federal tax law, business owners and people responsible for handling payroll must keep employee tax payments separate and hold them for the government. Using this money for personal expenses or business costs instead is a federal crime.Federal sentencing and restitution orderAfter her conviction, a federal judge sentenced Butdorf to 18 months in prison. She will also face a period of supervised release after completing her sentence. The judge also ordered her to repay the Internal Revenue Service in full for the unpaid taxes that built up over the six-year period. Assistant United States Attorney Megan R. Miller handled the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio. Federal authorities stressed that failing to pay employment taxes can harm workers by putting their future Social Security and Medicare benefits at risk. They also said that businesses that avoid paying these taxes gain an unfair advantage over companies that follow federal tax laws. The case was handled in coordination with the Department of Justice's National Fraud Enforcement Division. This initiative works with federal law enforcement agencies to investigate and tackle financial fraud and tax-related crimes across the country.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: For the first time, Sonia confirms battle with cancer in memoirs
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Sonia Gandhi's memoirs, released on Tuesday, officially acknowledge what was long whispered within political circles but never publicly
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Sonia Gandhi's memoirs, released on Tuesday, officially acknowledge what was long whispered within political circles but never publicly confirmed - her battle with cancer, which occurred during the second term of UPA govt.They also set the record straight on where her two surgeries took place - first at European Institute of Oncology, near Milan in Italy, and later at Erasmus University Medical Centre in Rotterdam - and not at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, as was widely speculated.According to Sonia, while she had suffered from occasional bouts of asthma and allergies, she had no serious health troubles until 2010, when she was advised to undergo surgery for suspected breast cancer. She chose not to get operated on in India as she wanted to avoid a media frenzy.‘I saw Rajiv reaching out to me, smiling at me’After much discussion with her doctors, Sonia Gandhi opted to get operated on by Dr Veronesi, a celebrated surgeon who was the founder and head of the European Institute.In her book, ‘Belonging: A Journey of Love’, Sonia writes, “On the day of the surgery, as I was wheeled into the operation theatre, Rahul and Priyanka held my hand and kissed me on the forehead, assuring me that all would be well. Afterwards, still groggy from the anaesthesia, I saw Dr Veronesi with them by my bedside. How relieved I felt to hear him announce, ‘Non c’è niente da preoccuparsi, tutto è andato bene e non ci sono residui. (No need to worry, everything has gone well and there are no residues).’ He had removed two tumours, including a non-suspicious one to be on the safe side, and conducted an intra-operative radiation to spare me five weeks of radiotherapy.”However, a year later, routine follow-up tests detected a growth in the pancreas. This time Sonia was sent to Erasmus, to be treated by a well-known pancreatic surgeon, Dr Casper van Eijck. Again, Rahul and Priyanka were by her side before the surgery. When she woke up, dazed and parched, she heard them calling out, “Ma, Mama, all is well — nothing bad!” The doctor later explained that fortunately, the tumour was found in a preliminary precancerous stage, having been detected early.Sonia also mentions that in Aug 2016, she collapsed during a long roadshow in hot and humid weather in Varanasi and broke her shoulder in the fall, forcing her to undergo another operation.
